articles.title_orig: Discovery of Exquisite Feathered Dinosaur in China Could Rewrite The Evolution of Flight
articles.title_zh: Discovery of Exquisite Feathered Dinosaur in China Could Rewrite The Evolution of Flight
articles.content_orig:
An exquisitely preserved feathered raptor just discovered in north-eastern China could probably fly.
It's also somewhat disrupted the evolutionary path we thought birds took to get into the air.
Norellraptor barsboldi, as the new dinosaur has been named, is a microraptor, which means it's a small dinosaur with feathers and wings.
It's also a member of the wider group Paraves , which includes a range of theropod dinosaurs , including some that are still thriving today: birds.
And, like its living relatives, Norellraptor could probably fly.
But close analysis of this remarkably detailed fossil suggests the evolutionary path to flight may be far more forked than we thought.
Norellraptor is described in a new paper by paleontologist Xuri Wang of the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and his colleagues. The paper is published in Nature Communications .
The microraptor's body is 57 centimeters long (just over 22 inches), and based on its bones, the researchers think it hadn't quite finished growing at the time of its death.
Its feathers are much less well-preserved than its bones, but from what the researchers could see, its forelimbs and tail seem to have been festooned with flight-related plumage, while other parts of its body were covered in straight, simple feathers.
Certain features in this Norellraptor's bones, and a close look at where it sits in the Paraves family tree has led the researchers to question what we know about how flight evolved within Paraves.
The fact that both microraptors and birds evolved the ability to fly doesn't necessarily mean they inherited the trait from the same ancestor.
Norellraptor 's current position in the Paraves family tree suggests flight may have actually arisen at least twice, independently.
The steps it followed to reach the skies seem to be quite different from those taken by birds.
Another bit of evidence is that the development of the dinosaur's forearm, or wing, seems to have stopped quite early in its life, which is the opposite of what we see in modern, flying birds.
"The sequences of flight-related novelties reconstructed along the two lineages differ consistently," Wang and team write .
"Combined with histological evidence which might indicate a peculiar limb growth model in Microraptorinae, these results dismiss a shared developmental pattern driving the evolution of the flying dinosaurs and support multiple and independent selective regimes at the origin of the winged taxa in Paraves."
In other words, there might have been some convergent evolution going on in the Paraves family.
That's when two separate evolutionary groups reach a similar outcome via a totally different route. Think whales and fishes: both can swim using fins, but they arrived at that body plan from totally different paths.
Still, paleontologists can't rely on just one fossil to rewrite evolutionary history.
A lot more evidence will be needed before scientists are convinced that birds and microraptors did indeed evolve flight entirely independently.
"Microraptorines have been advocated as models for investigating the origin and evolution of the avian flight," the authors note .
"Yet, the evolutionary relationships between the flight apparatus of birds and the purported aerial adaptations of the microraptorines are controversial from both functional and phylogenetic perspectives."
The research has been published in Nature Communications .

articles.title_orig: Reflecting Pool vandalism charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn permanently dismissed
articles.title_zh: Reflecting Pool vandalism charges against Olympic canoeist David Hearn permanently dismissed
articles.content_orig:
A Washington, D.C., judge permanently dismissed the criminal indictment against U.S. Olympic canoeist David Hearn Thursday, ending a months-long saga around allegations of vandalism to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool after the government admitted to a "botched" construction job in recent renovations.
In August, federal prosecutors asked Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman to dismiss the criminal indictment against Hearn, who had been charged with felony destruction of government property. He was accused of causing more than $1,000 in damage to the sealant that was installed last summer at the bottom of the Reflecting Pool.
Hearn pleaded not guilty to the charges, saying he had stopped by the pool in July while on a 64-mile bike ride through the nation's capital. He said he was arrested after he reached down into the pool and was detained for five hours.
The project to renovate the pool has been championed by President Trump, who in April launched an effort to address the pool's "terrible" condition, part of a slate of spring cleaning projects in Washington, D.C., ahead of the nation's 250th birthday. He had the pool's stone flooring coated with a sealant he called the "latest and greatest filament" and an "industrial-grade" variation of swimming pool liner. He told reporters he personally chose the sealant's color: "American Flag Blue."
The U.S. Attorney's Office in D.C. admitted in court filings that Hearn had not, in fact, damaged the pool, although U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro alleged in a July press conference that he had. Prosecutors said new information had come to light revealing the rips and tears in the pool lining were caused by a contractor's "botched installation."
Edelman dismissed the case shortly after the government's motion, but had not ruled on whether the case would be dismissed with prejudice, meaning the case could not be brought again, or without prejudice, meaning the charges could be revived. Hearn's lawyers said the charges should be dismissed with prejudice, while Pirro's office argued for a dismissal without prejudice.
Hearn's case, Edelman wrote , "presents a markedly different scenario" than the typical dismissal of criminal cases in federal court, because "within a month, the government recognized that its prosecution lacked merit."
"It reached this conclusion not because it has misidentified Mr. Hearn as the perpetrator of the alleged act, but because no crime had occurred," Edelman wrote, adding that the government's interest in keeping the possibility of charging Hearn again would result in a "meritless, politically motivated prosecution."
After Pirro's office moved to drop the case, Mr. Trump publicly rebuked his hand-picked D.C. prosecutor, saying that she had "choked" and "made a mistake" with the decision.
"I was disappointed with Jeanine Pirro," Mr. Trump told reporters in August. The president has frequently insisted the peeling was caused by vandals, not by problems with the more than $10 million project. "Who would do such a thing?" the president wrote in a Truth Social post on June 20 that also mentioned several arrests . Many of the other defendants accused of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool also had the charges against them dropped .
Pirro later made a bid to prove to Mr. Trump that the damage to the Reflecting Pool was caused by the shoddy construction job, bringing a box full of evidence to the White House that sources said contained all of the evidence collected from the Interior Department exculpating Hearn and several others from criminal vandalism.
The New York Times in September reported that the contractor, Atlantic Industrial Coatings, admitted in government documents that the workers had not used enough primer and that the pool liner that was applied contained two chemicals that were incompatible.
Days after Pirro's office moved to dismiss the case, CBS News reported that White House officials asked the Justice Department to weigh whether it would be possible to bring a new criminal case against Hearn.
In a statement, Norm Eisen, an attorney for Hearn, said that Edelman's ruling is "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice."
"This case never should have been brought in the first place," Eisen said, adding that the prosecution was a "miscarriage of justice" and an "outrage that should shock every American."
A spokesperson for Pirro's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Edelman's decision.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Tennessee Inmate in Critical Condition After ‘Torturous’ Botched Execution, Lawyer Says
articles.content_orig:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survived the state's attempt to execute her Wednesday night when the lethal injection failed . She was transported to an area hospital, where she remained alive on Thursday, according to her attorneys, who said she was receiving "lifesaving medical care." They said they don't know her prognosis.
"All of this was predicted, and the court did nothing," said one of Pike's attorneys, Steve Ferrell, referencing the state's past issues carrying out lethal injections.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee called off the remaining scheduled execution in the state this year and ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred," he said in a statement Thursday.
Pike, who was convicted of a 1995 murder, was slated to be the first woman executed in Tennessee in the last 200 years after the Supreme Court ruled earlier Wednesday that her execution could proceed.
Correctional staff gave Pike two doses of the lethal drug pentobarbital at around 8 p.m. local time Wednesday, but she still had a heartbeat, had not lost consciousness and was "audibly snoring" when her attorneys filed an emergency motion to halt the procedure later in the night, according to the filing.
Close to an hour after the execution began, at 8:53 p.m. local time, there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area, the Associated Press reported. Attorneys for Pike noted in the emergency motion that the curtain in the execution chamber had gone down twice during the ordeal.
"Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State's most serious responsibilities," Lee said in his statement, "and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective."
The Tennessee Department of Correction said it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office. The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."
In a news conference late Wednesday night, AP reporter Kim Chandler, one of the media witnesses to the attempted execution, said that at one point Pike "looked toward prison officials and asked if it was supposed to feel that way."
"Her mouth fell open a few times, and she began to loudly snore," Chandler recounted, noting that the snoring continued for several minutes.
According to Chandler, the blinds to the execution chamber closed for the final time at about 8:06 p.m. When media witnesses were asked to leave the area at about 8:53 p.m., Pike could still be heard "loudly snoring, clearly very alive."
Will Puckett, a reporter for CBS affiliate WVLT, another of the media witnesses, said that after the curtain closed for the final time, "You could hear doors opening and closing. Her lawyers were in and out. Her spiritual adviser was in and out from that point. And then at 8:53, the mic was cut off after the warden said, 'Will the witnesses please exit the area.'"
In a supplemental court filing from Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti, state officials said that Pike had been transported to a hospital where she was "receiving medical care." The court filing did not provide details on her condition or which hospital she was taken to.
"Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution," Pike's attorneys said in a statement provided to CBS News. "We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms. Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy. Christa is being treated at a nearby hospital. We have not been informed as to her condition."
This all comes after the Supreme Court earlier Wednesday overrode a last-minute district court order to halt Pike's execution. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented.
Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death at 10 a.m. local time Wednesday at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit ruled that a "short" pause on the execution proceedings was needed to resolve new claims from Pike's legal team.
"The Court's decision to vacate that stay interferes with the Sixth Circuit's routine administrative handling of a capital case and unnecessarily prevents that court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim," Sotomayor wrote in her dissent.
Pike's attorneys had argued that counsel in her initial criminal case failed to properly introduce her extensive childhood experiences with abuse into their defense and was therefore ineffective.
"I am not afraid to die. I'm only nervous about the process," wrote Pike earlier this week, in a letter she penned before Lee denied her clemency petition and cleared the way for her execution to take place.
Thanking those who rallied for the governor to intervene and halt the plan, Pike said she was "at peace," regardless of the outcome of her bid. CBS News obtained a copy of the letter from her spiritual adviser, Rev. Mikey Noechel, along with a copy of another note Noechel received from Pike that contained handwritten lines from the poem "To ——" by Edgar Allan Poe. Noechel said he received the poem on Sunday and the letter on Monday.
Now 50, Pike has been incarcerated since 1995 for the murder that year of her former classmate, Colleen Slemmer. According to court records, Pike and Slemmer were students at the Job Corps Center in Knoxville when Pike, then 18, tortured and killed her, allegedly over comments Slemmer, 19, had made about her relationship.
Pike's boyfriend and another friend helped carry out the attack and murder, the records said.
Pike's case has drawn international attention and some outcry, with the United Nations recently joining local advocacy groups in their calls for Lee to commute her death sentence .
Their criticisms mainly center on the childhood abuse and untreated mental illness from which Pike suffered when Slemmer was killed, factors that play much larger roles in how juries make sentencing decisions now than they did at Pike's trial. U.N. experts also said the decades Pike spent in isolation on death row, as the sole woman awaiting execution in Tennessee, should amount to unlawful torture.
Once Lee announced the clemency bid had been rejected, Pike's attorneys issued a statement saying they were "deeply saddened and heartbroken" by the news. In it, they noted how much their client had changed while incarcerated.
"The 18-year-old girl suffering from severe mental illness and near-debilitating trauma no longer exists," the statement said. "Christa is a 50-year-old remorseful woman who understands her actions, receives proper treatment for her mental illness, and provides for and guides fellow incarcerated women."
One of her attorneys, Luke Ihnen, told CBS News that "in her classic Christa way, she has spent her last days worried more about her friends, family and legal team than herself."
In a statement included with her clemency petition , Pike said she recognized that the ramifications of her crime have been "huge, unforgettable and ruined countless lives."
"It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected," she said. "I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
Prosecutors and jurors in Pike's initial criminal case, as well as the judges who presided over that trial and her numerous appeals, have often described Slemmer's murder as brutal and horrific. Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, told the Knoxville News-Sentinel after Pike's conviction in 1996 that she believed Pike was "evil," and the state "should kill her right away."

articles.title_orig: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.title_zh: Global bond rout deepens, pushes US Treasury yields to 24-year peak
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields fell on Thursday, giving back some of the recent gains that propelled longer-dated rates to levels not seen in decades.
The 10-year Treasury yield breached a level last seen in April 2002, before easing 5 basis points to 5.243%. The 10-year influences rates on mortgage and auto loans and credit card debt. The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond also hit its highest in 24 years before dropping more than 2 basis points to 5.613%.
Yields and prices move inversely. One basis point equals 0.01%.
Jeff Kilburg, CEO of KKM Financial, said he sees the 10-year yield pulling back to around 4.5%-4.75% if the U.S. and Iran can reach a deal to end the war. "If we're going to continue to stay in Iran, then that's going to be problematic for the 10-year yield."
Government borrowing costs around the world continued their relentless march upward on Thursday, continuing a monthslong trend as investors voted with their feet over a lack of political will to tackle fiscal deficits, while inflation remains stubbornly above target and leading central banks move to push interest rates higher.
Major economies face "persistently large deficits and rising interest expenses — challenges long associated with debt-distressed emerging market sovereigns," the Institute of International Finance said last week .
Japan's 10-year yield hit its highest level since the mid-1990s. Japan's debt has come under pressure from a weaker yen and rate hikes by the Bank of Japan .
The yield on the German 10-year bund, the benchmark for the euro area, topped 3.6%, the highest since 2008, before easing back. Elsewhere in Europe, the French 10-year surged 8 basis points to 4.925%, Italy's 10-year was up 10 basis points to 4.706%, while the U.K.'s 10-year yield increased 5 basis points to 5.483%.
"It's worth noting, but people get pretty worked up about those sorts of spreads regularly, so I don't think it's a crisis point necessarily, as far as Germany versus France or Italy," said Michael Schumacher, former managing director at Wells Fargo. "If you look at some countries that have very poor structural dynamics, like the UK, and I'd be concerned about that. People don't typically trade gilts versus bunds as much, but just as a barometer of, say, market concern, I think that's one to watch."
Bonds had been moving in lockstep with oil prices , which have been turbulent as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran obstructed crude exports from the Middle East. Crude oil prices were higher on Thursday , with international benchmark Brent crude futures back above $100 a barrel.
"We could see [bond] buyers come in effectively to take advantage of those yields, which would have the effect of causing them to go down, but also one of the things that has kept the volatility in those yields in the long end of the curve has been what's going on with oil, what's going on with inflation," Nomi Prins, founder of Prinsights Global, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
But sovereign wealth funds and central banks, among the main long-term holders of Treasury debt, are unlikely to go along, Prins said.
"We could see movement ... in Treasury yields going down if oil prices go down significantly, if there's a resolution" in the Middle East, Prins added.
— With additional reporting from CNBC's Jeff Cox

articles.title_orig: Boeing Engineers Bless New Contract After Summer Showdown
articles.title_zh: Boeing Engineers Bless New Contract After Summer Showdown
articles.content_orig:
Boeing engineers and technical workers approved a sweetened four-year contract with immediate 10% raises, avoiding a potential strike at the aerospace giant as it seeks federal approval for new aircraft and to increase aircraft production.
"We secured many victories that some thought were completely out of reach when this negotiation cycle started," said the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace, which represents about 13,000 Boeing engineers and 4,000 technical workers.
Boeing increased its offer in mid-September after the workers rejected an earlier proposal. In addition to the 10% ratification wage increase, the four-year contract includes annual raises of 4%, with an increase of up to 6% based on merit.
The professional unit, which includes engineers, voted 67.62% in favor of the new contract, and the tech unit approved the contract with 53.48% in favor, the union said.
The work groups, which make up Boeing's largest white-collar union, overwhelmingly rejected an earlier offer with 3% annual raises.
Boeing said in a statement that it was "pleased with the outcome of the vote."
The approval lets Boeing avoid a strike just as it's trying to stabilize and increase production of its fast-selling jets and win federal approval for the 737 Max 10 and 777X, which are years behind schedule.
The Federal Aviation Administration on Monday said it's assessing whether a software issue on the 737 Max 10, which could affect landing procedures in certain scenarios, poses a safety of flight issue.
A machinist strike two years ago halted production until the two sides reached a deal.

articles.title_orig: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting
articles.title_zh: Renee Good's family sues Trump administration over fatal Minneapolis shooting
articles.content_orig:
The family of Renee Good, one of two US citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in the state of Minnesota, has sued the government over her killing during a sweeping immigrant deportation blitz in January.
The two lawsuits – filed on Thursday by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger – say officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration were reckless and violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis. The lawsuits are demanding a jury trial and financial damages.
The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
The first lawsuit seeks damages for Good’s wrongful death under Minnesota law, citing claims of assault, battery, false imprisonment, negligence and intentional infliction of emotional distress.
The second lawsuit alleges a civil rights conspiracy among numerous defendants including the immigration officer and shooter Jonathon Ross, who was named alongside high-ranking Trump administration officials, including White House Deputy Policy Chief Stephen Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, former Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and Trump’s longtime campaign adviser, Corey Lewandowski.
Good, a mother of three, was shot and killed in her car by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent in south Minneapolis when she and her wife joined one of the city’s daily demonstrations against masked and armed federal agents deployed to the city to arrest migrants for deportation.
Widespread cellphone footage taken by eyewitnesses captured the moment in which Good was killed, after agent Ross fired into the windshield, shooting her in the head, arm and torso.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.
In a statement posted on Truth Social at the time, Trump defended the deadly ICE shooting, saying that the reason those “incidents” were happening was that “the Radical Left is threatening, assaulting, and targeting our Law Enforcement Officers and ICE Agents on a daily basis”.
Days after the shooting, officials from the US Department of Justice, including then-Deputy Attorney Todd Blanche, blocked federal prosecutors from pursuing a criminal civil rights case against the agents involved in her killing, which prompted at least half a dozen of those prosecutors to resign in protest.
Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.
None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.

articles.title_zh: Chris Hansen Confronts ‘Primetime’: The Tragic Ending, Seeing His Love Life Onscreen and Considering Legal Action Against A24 Because ‘They Exploited Me’
articles.content_orig:
By JOANNA TWEEDY, ASSISTANT EDITOR, LIFESTYLE & TRAVEL
Published: 06:22 EDT, 1 October 2026 | Updated: 07:08 EDT, 1 October 2026
Football pundit Chris 'Kammy' Kamara says This Morning presenter Ben Shephard helped to save him from a deep depression that saw him contemplating suicide – as  the former midfielder launches a new mental health campaign with Visit Guernsey.
Speaking from the Channel Island, where he unveiled the 'Here for C.H.R.I.S' initiative to encourage more men to ask for help, he tells the Daily Mail how he struggled for too long in silence with his own demons – and lost two close friends, Gary Speed and Ricky Hatton , to suicide.
The 68-year-old, who was diagnosed in 2022 with the neurological condition apraxia, which slows down both his speech and his thought processes, says the change in his health also sparked a devastating decline in his mental wellbeing.
The ex Soccer Saturday star says: 'I spent 18 months hiding it from my family. I had these dark thoughts, little voices going on inside the brain telling me "you're gonna be a burden".'
Research published by Visit Guernsey this week finds that more than a quarter of men across the UK are hesitant to discuss deteriorating mental health with family and friends. A third said they would feel more comfortable opening up in a safe place away from their usual environment, such as on holiday.
The findings have led the Channel Island's tourism office to partner with Guernsey Mind, launching the 'No man is an island' campaign and the Here for C.H.R.I.S initiative, the letters of which stand for 'calm, helpful, reassuring and inviting space'.
Chris Kamara has joined forces with Visit Guernsey to encourage men to seek help when they need it, launching a mental health initiative called Here for C.H.R.I.S
Kamara, 68, who was diagnosed with aspraxia and plunged into a deep depression during the pandemic, says This Morning star Ben Shephard persuaded him to open up and seek help
Explains Kamara: 'Y ou can walk into any bar, restaurant or other establishment on the island and say "I'm here for Chris" and trained staff will get someone to instantly help you. They'll give you a drink and get a mental health professional.'
He adds: 'I prefer to be called "Kammy", but in this instance, I'm Chris all the way.'
The football pundit's own experiences with depression, which took hold during the Covid pandemic in 2020, only stopped, he says, when he finally found a way to ask for help – and because a celebrity pal kept checking in on him.
'My family knew there was something up but as I wasn't speaking to anyone, they didn't know what was going on.
'I thought I would wake up one day and it would all be gone, but of course, every single day it gets harder and harder.'
He adds: 'I got well with Ben Shephard's help – he was marvellous. He kept phoning me up to see how I was and eventually I saw a therapist.'
Kamara says he's experienced the devastating consequences of men not asking for help first hand after losing two 'big pals' to suicide, Ricky Hatton, left, and Gary Speed
Kamara, pictured playing for Sheffield United in 1993, says he worried people might turn their backs on him or become judgemental if he revealed his mental health struggles
The This Morning star recommended a treatment that his former GMTV co-star Kate Garraway had sought out for her late husband Derek Draper in Monterrey, Mexico and persuaded Kamara to try it .
The breakthrough therapy at the NeuroCytonix clinic saw him receive experimental magnetic field and radio frequency treatment, which he says 'helped me immensely.'
Having seen former Wales manager Gary Speed and boxing hero Ricky Hatton both die by suicide, he's determined to use his own experience and the loss of his two friends to try and help other men – and is fully behind Visit Guernsey's efforts to ensure there's designated safe spaces on the island for those who need help. He hopes the project will roll out across the UK.
'I lost two close friends. Gary Speed and Ricky Hatton were my two big pals. I played with Gary at Leeds and Ricky had an apartment in Spain across from mine, so we met up every single year for 15 years.
'W hen Ricky died, he seemed in as good a shape mentally as I've known him for a while but you don't know. You've got no idea what's going on inside someone's head, unless they tell you.'
At the root of his own depression was the idea that people would judge him for his slower speech.
Visit Guernsey, the Channel Island's tourism office, is encouraging younger male travellers to stay on the island and enjoy a relaxing break, as they raise awareness about mental wellness
He says: 'I was frightened. I thought that once I revealed I was going through stuff, people might turn their backs on me. It was the opposite, and that's what we want to say: speak to someone and there will be a way out.'
The commentator hasn't looked back on his own journey to mental wellness, saying: ' I have a new lease of life. How I ever got to that dark place, I'll never know, but the brain is so complex. But now I'm out of it, I think, I'm in a position now to help people, and that's the important thing.'
Sam Claxton, Marketing Manager at VisitGuernsey said of the campaign: 'It’s been fantastic working with and learning from Guernsey Mind on this initiative as we understand that the issue of increasing mental health challenges is not going anywhere.
'"Here for C.H.R.I.S" is part of our wider ‘No Man is an Island’ campaign where we’re actively encouraging younger male travellers – a growing audience for us – to visit the island and enjoy a much needed break.
'Working with Chris has been incredible. He is the perfect person to be involved in this campaign, given how openly he has shared his own experiences and his background in professional sport, an environment where there is a strong stigma around these issues.'
The ex footballer's first time on Guernsey to launch the campaign hasn't disappointed either, Kamara says: 'I told my wife last night "I went to the best restaurant on the island", and I'll be telling her today we've got to come back because it's beautiful.'
Find out more about the Here for C.H.R.I.S campaign at visitguernsey.com.
Call the Samaritans for free, confidential support 24/7 at 116 123 (in the UK).

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says investigations suggest the man who stabbed his fellow pilot and tried to take over a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination".
The Flydubai plane plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two hours into its journey on Wednesday, before passengers and crew overpowered the attacker and retook control to land safely.
Netanyahu told Fox News that it was looking "very likely" that the attacker, who he said was an Omani national, "was going to down the plane".
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) state news agency reports investigations have begun there to determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose".
The Interior Ministry of Saudi Arabia - where the plane made an emergency landing - said that both the pilot and co-pilot had been sent back to the UAE on Thursday morning after medical teams had cleared them.
UAE officials earlier claimed jurisdiction over the incident because the aircraft on which the attack took place is registered there and flies under its flag.
Netanyahu told Fox that once the attacker had been subdued and tied up by passengers and crew, he was "calling out to the aircrew 'kill me, kill me', so it's clear he was suicidal - that's not a question".
Passenger Almog Itali said it felt like a "rollercoaster" as Flight FZ1073 fell 17,000ft in less than two minutes
"And with all the passengers in there, and if you couple that with what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that were found in his background, I think... that'll give us a pretty good clue."
However, he stressed that he did not want to draw any firm conclusions as to motive yet.
Both US President Donald Trump and UAE officials have indicated to the media that Iran may be responsible for the incident, without definitively blaming Tehran.
Trump told reporters on Thursday that Iran would be "hit very hard" if it was deemed to have been involved in the attack.
Pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel were usually not allowed to fly there, Netanyahu said when asked about how the suspected Omani pilot came to be on the plane.
He added: "Obviously there was a loophole here and we're taking care of that among other things... with the full co-operation, I have to say, of the Emirati government, so we're both interested in making sure this doesn't happen again."
Oman has not formally established official ties with Israel , unlike the UAE.
The prime minister was also asked earlier on the same network whether there was an indication if Iran was involved, he replied: "It's too early to say".
Flydubai passenger describes hugging his children as plane nosedived during attack
Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
Both Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the stabbed pilot, Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar was a "hero".
India's ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Captain Machhar in hospital on Thursday, the Indian Mission confirmed on social media, stating he was "in good health and recovering well".
The Indian government has praised Smit Machchhar for his "immense courage"
Preliminary findings from a separate Israeli investigation into the incident, suggest that the alleged attacker intended to crash the plane, an Israeli security source told BBC Arabic.
The source said the investigation - led by Israel's intelligence agency Mossad - interviewed passengers after they arrived in Tel Aviv to establish what had happened on the plane.
Flydubai's flight FZ1073, with more than 170 people on board, took off from Dubai International Airport in the UAE at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time), en route to Ben Gurion Airport.
Two hours later, the 17,000ft drop in altitude was reported on the plane tracking website Flightradar24 and minutes later the plane signalled an emergency code.
At about 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent, landing safely at  Tabuk Airport in the north west of Saudi.
Flydubai has since suspended flights between Dubai and Tel Aviv as it carried out its own investigation into the incident.
Israel's Transportation Ministry said the suspension aligns with Netanyahu's directive.
Israeli airlines including El Al, Israir and Arkia said plans were in place to operate rescue flights from Dubai starting on Friday to bring back stranded passengers.
The Transportation Ministry also said it sent an urgent request to Etihad Airlines to increase the number of flights between Abu Dhabi and Tel Aviv.

U.K. police say they arrested multiple suspects for offenses under the "Explosives Act" near a U.S. airbase in southwest England on Sunday.
Gloucestershire Police say the arrests took place just two miles from RAF Fairford, which hosts U.S. Air Force assets. The U.S. has recently used the base in operations relating to the war in Iran.
"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."

"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles," police added.
President Donald Trump responded to news of the arrests while talking to the press later Sunday.
"The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain. It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation," Trump said of the suspects. "They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great."
A reporter then asked if the suspects were migrants, and Trump demurred.
"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know that we worked with a lot of them. We had them under review for a long time and we got them," Trump said.
Authorities did not name the suspects or detail exactly how many were arrested.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting wrote on X that the situation is "being dealt with."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham also released a statement on the arrests.
"I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country. My thanks go to Gloucestershire Police, Counter Terrorism Policing, our Armed Forces and all those working to keep the public safe," he said.
"The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe. The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts," he added.
WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES
The incident comes roughly a month after Iran-linked hackers were suspected of forcing a small British power generator offline for several days this summer.
The British shutdown came weeks after hackers struck more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota , accessing technology used to remotely monitor and control pumps and other equipment. Minnesota officials have not publicly attributed the attacks. Several news outlets, citing U.S. officials and a leaked industry threat-sharing memo, reported that Iran was the likely culprit.

articles.title_orig: Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Cleveland Browns Matchup Breakdown For Fantasy Football Week 4
articles.title_zh: Pittsburgh Steelers vs. Cleveland Browns Matchup Breakdown For Fantasy Football Week 4
articles.content_orig:
John Laghezza breaks down the Week 4 Thursday Night Football tilt between the Browns and Steelers for fantasy football.
Nothing says “get the leather helmets, this is old-school fall football” like Browns versus Steelers in Cleveland, with a sub-39-point total on the board. Two teams are trying to convince the world their winning records are real, and regardless of your thoughts, one’s leaving in a great spot to make a run at the second season.
I’m not crying over the Bengals’ loss to the Steelers, you are. Fine, maybe I am too. And not to say old man Aaron Rodgers still can’t sling a pretty deep ball (oh boy, can he), but without several game-changing errors, we’re telling a completely different story heading into Week 4.
You’d think a quarterback with the sixth-highest number of dropbacks/game (40.7) would spur more fantasy interest, but this black-and-yellow passing game’s still an avoid for me. Rodgers went for (292-3-1) on Sunday, despite completing just 56% of passes — without a single pass-catcher earning more than six targets or reeling in a fourth grab. No thanks.
DK Metcalf finally found the end zone, and still runs every possible route — but that doesn’t quite paper over the rotten advanced metrics for his draft-day cost (19.2% target/route, 0.78 yards/route). The return of Michael Pittman hurts everyone as well, especially if Mike McCarthy’s going to keep dialing up specialized high-value plays for Ben Skowronek and Darnell Washington that help absolutely no one.
Speaking of the latter, no matter how much fun watching the behemoth known as Darnell Washington swatting defenders running downfield is, that same action will cannibalize the TE1-type volume going Pat Freiermuth 's way. The Muth’s still startable for now, but I’d start looking for replacements due to target sharing — namely this new chemistry building with Roman Wilson . Yes, the former third-round post-hype sleeper out of Michigan took over the every-down role in 11-personnel, earning six targets/game, responsible for the NFL’s 11th-most unrealized air yards. Timing starts in fantasy will be tough, but there’s potentially contingency/dynasty value here.
Pittsburgh shelved Rico Dowdle with a balky toe, which opened up the floodgates for Jaylen Warren . Finally allowed to shine as a solo act, Warren soaked up 90% of backfield opportunities and 100% of the production (20 touches, 176 scrimmage yards). Dowdle’s status remains up in the air after back-to-back DNPs, and chances he could play are waning to avoid being too risky given the short turnaround.
Warren’s a start regardless, as well as a decent buy-high asset for the non-zero chance of leaving Dowdle in his fantasy dust. Not to mention it’s an ugly divisional game against a Browns’ D bottom-5 in yards after contact/carry (3.35) and explosive rush rate (10.0%). Looks like the long-awaited Warren breakout could finally be upon us.
To all the Browns backers out there, especially those big Deshaun Watson fans (do those exist?), I’m sorry. I was definitely wrong, not only about Cleveland’s viability as a collective but Watson’s athletic ability coming off a second Achilles injury. Difficult to not come away at least somewhat impressed with his ability to escape and turn the usual sack into a sensational first down — one run in the first quarter particularly reminded me of his glory days in Houston.
In spite of all my roses thrown at Watson’s feet already, there’s still plenty to be concerned about before making moves to start him in fantasy. For starters, the off-target rate's still through the roof (14.6%), while an extremely shallow air yards/attempt (6.0) spurns the league’s worst rate of throws beyond the marker (28.6%). Are things better than expected? Yes. But are they good? No.
Usually, low-aDOT attacks with a running quarterback calling shots throw a wet blanket on most, if not all, associated fantasy assets. However, there’s an attention-worthy amount of consolidation going on here, especially if your team’s been bitten by the injury bug. Watson attempted 30 passes Sunday, targeting just three total WR/TEs: KC Concepcion (9), Harold Fannin (9), and Denzel Boston (4). Start the first two in PPR with some degree of confidence, with Boston’s deep-threat role (5 targets/game, 80 air yards/game) making him a boom-or-bust play for fantasy.
I wish I could share the same optimism for the Browns’ backfield … but can’t. Just when we thought Quinshon Judkins started on his way to a truly featured role, earning more pass game work by catching five balls in Week 2 — we get the rug pulled out from under us. Sad trombone sounds all around.
Having to rely purely on rushing points behind an objectively bad O-line, responsible for what’s easily a bottom-5 ground attack (-0.31 EPA/rush, 3.5 yards/attempt, 40.0% success, 4.0% explosive rush rate) will keep Judkins relegated to the RB3 discussion. Startable, but capped as long as Raheim Sanders suits up.
Forced to choose between the two two-win teams I believe in the least wasn’t easy. Pittsburgh’s front seven creates enough pressure to sufficiently disrupt the inaccurate Watson, and the Browns’ man-heavy approach struggles to defend Rodgers’ play-action ball fakes in a narrow loss.

Two years after a woman alleged a gang rape at Cornell University, renewed attention to the case and the limited consequences faced by the alleged perpetrators has raised questions about what higher education owes students who experience sexual assault on campus as well as how consent and intoxication are understood under New York law.
A woman identified as Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging that she was sexually assaulted, gang-raped, and pressured to take drugs and drink alcohol by seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity on the night of Oct. 19, 2024. The lawsuit is filed against the fraternity, Doe’s sorority chapter, and Cornell University; it names Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris, and Scott Kretzschmar as defendants. Prosecutors said this week they were reopening a criminal investigation into the case after declining to press charges originally.
Separate attorneys for Kretzschmar and Lopes denied the allegations in statements to ABC , while Norris, via an attorney, denied engaging in sexual activity or drug use but acknowledged that he sent a message included in the complaint.
When sexual assault allegations of this kind occur on campus, they can be addressed in three distinct ways: through school disciplinary proceedings, criminal proceedings, and civil lawsuits.
Doe’s civil lawsuit alleges that Cornell failed to protect her. Her attorney has separately criticized authorities’ handling of the criminal investigation, although observers say what’s known as the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in state law could limit what prosecutors are able to charge.
Here’s what to know about how the case was handled—by Cornell and the criminal justice system—before, and what could happen next.
Doe reported the alleged assault to campus police in November 2024. According to her complaint, Cornell began its Title IX investigation on Jan. 14, 2025.
Title IX is a law dating back to 1972 that is meant to, among other things, ensure that a college investigates when there is sexual assault on campus. Central to this premise is that Title IX is meant to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
Read More: Trump’s Title IX Announcement Is Cruel. But It Does Not Change the Law
Doe’s attorney has said that Cornell expelled two of the seven accused students. Cornell has confirmed that its disciplinary process resulted in expulsions and suspensions, but has not disclosed individual outcomes. The lawsuit alleges negligence, breach of contract, and violations of New York law.
Cornell responded in a statement last week, saying that it could not confirm the individual disciplinary outcomes due to student privacy laws. However, the university clarified on Monday that “none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
“We take sexual violence extremely seriously,” the Sept. 21 statement said. “The Presidential Task Force on Campus Sexual Assault was launched shortly after this incident and issued a REPORT in March 2026.”
In a statement Monday, Kyle Kimball, Cornell’s vice president for university relations, said Chi Phi’s Cornell chapter closed in 2024 and the fraternity remains barred from campus.
But women’s rights advocates believe that the school might not have fulfilled its legal obligations in investigating the incident and taking appropriate actions toward those involved.
Title IX is a federal civil rights law meant to prohibit sex-based discrimination in any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.
Since Title IX was introduced, courts have found that the law requires institutions to ensure that sexual violence does not impede a student’s access to education.
“The reason why Title IX addresses sexual harassment, including sexual assault, is because of the very real impact that has on students’ ability to access education,” Shiwali Patel, a Title IX expert with the National Women’s Law Center, tells TIME.
According to the Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network (RAINN), students who experience sexual assault are more likely to earn lower GPAs in school and are more likely to drop out of school altogether.
Patel points to Doe’s attorney’s account of her efforts to leave Cornell after the alleged assault. In a Sept. 28 interview with CNN, Thomas Giuffra—Jane Doe’s lawyer—said Cornell refused her family’s tuition-refund request, leaving her to spend another semester on campus.
“She was trying to leave the institution; she didn’t want to be there,” Patel says.
Cornell told People that it works with students seeking to take leave or withdraw and “regularly refunds payments if students are no longer enrolled.”
Giuffra also told CNN that Doe is no longer in college as of 2026.
Universities also have obligations to offer support regardless of a formal complaint or a finding of culpability. These can include counseling, academic adjustments, and housing or schedule changes. Patel says it remains unclear whether Cornell fully complied with its Title IX obligations because the supportive measures it provided Doe are not publicly known.
Regardless, the situation raises questions about what more schools can do for students, Patel says, providing some examples of the types of questions that a university might ask in the aftermath of this kind of incident: “Does she need extensions on exams? Does she need some time off, some leave? Does she need a housing shift if the fraternity house and her sorority house are close together? Does she need counseling? Did they provide a stay away order? What kind of support were they giving her to make sure she wouldn’t have to be retriggered and traumatized by running into them?”
Title IX also requires schools to investigate allegations through a reliable, impartial process—independently of criminal court systems, and using a lower burden of proof to determine if a student violated campus policy.
Cornell University publicly disclosed that it was investigating the allegation on Nov. 8, 2024, the same day Doe went to the police, according to the lawsuit. The university sent an alert to students regarding a report of sexual assault and coercion into taking drugs at a fraternity house. The same day, Cornell suspended the Chi Phi fraternity.
In response to an inquiry from TIME, Cornell said that its “Office of Civil Rights and the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards investigated the allegations against the individuals and the fraternity consistent with university policies and Title IX.”
“The university’s Title IX investigation was conducted over several months and included hearings where a panel of trained faculty and staff heard evidence over multiple days,” the university’s statement continued. “The complainant and respondents had the opportunity to testify and present evidence in the university’s investigation.”
Cornell’s handling of the case unfolded amid shifting federal rules on campus sexual misconduct. A court vacated the Biden Administration’s Title IX rule on Jan. 9, 2025—five days before Cornell began its formal investigation, according to Doe’s complaint. The university held hearings that May, making the rules it applied a key question in assessing its response.
The Biden Administration had expanded Title IX regulations in April 2024—taking effect in August 2024—broadening the definition of sexual harassment and extending federal protections.

articles.title_orig: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.title_zh: Renée Good’s family sues Trump officials, saying death was ‘not an accident’
articles.content_orig:
The family of an American woman shot and killed by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent has filed two civil lawsuits related to her death, according to court records filed Thursday in Minnesota federal court.
Renee Good was killed January 7 by ICE agent Jonathan Ross in Minneapolis during the height of the Department of Homeland Security’s Operation Metro Surge, prompting significant protest in the city and sparking national outrage.
“The hole in my family and myself, created by my sister’s passing, is hauntingly apparent,” Good’s brother and plaintiff, Brent Ganger, said at a Thursday news conference announcing the lawsuits.
“Since Renee’s death, no meaningful change has occurred. The deaths of innocent Americans by taxpayer-funded government agents should not be a partisan issue, and it should alarm every American.”
One lawsuit names the United States of America as the sole defendant under the Federal Tort Claims Act , a federal law that allows people to sue the US government for personal injury, property damage or death, caused by alleged negligence of federal employees acting within their job duties.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory damages for Good’s partner, who witnessed the shooting, and “for the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” the family’s attorneys said in a statement.
We're tracking shootings, arrests and deportations in Trump's immigration crackdown. Here's the latest
In January, attorneys sent letters to the federal agencies connected with Good’s death, notifying them of their intention to pursue legal action. Under FTCA guidelines, they waited six months for a response, which could be a denial, agreement to payment, or simply a non-response, attorney Sarah Raisch said.
“We are here today because we have not heard from the government, either that they will accept the claim, or not,” attorney Antonio Romanucci said.
A tort lawsuit against the federal government, from guilt or innocence to the amount of a potential award, is typically decided by a federal judge.
In their second lawsuit, Good’s family alleges, among other things, Operation Metro Surge was “a carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors” to interfere with the civil rights of Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin, and to silence “the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented, and warned of that campaign.”
The suit names Ross, ten John Doe federal agents, and several current and former Trump administration officials as defendants, including White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, White House border czar Tom Homan, former Secretary of Homeland Security Kristi Noem, and Greg Bovino , the former Border Patrol official who led the administration’s immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis.
Lawyers for Renee Good’s family have experience taking on the government, but this time they face more hurdles
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the Trump administration intends “to vigorously defend these baseless civil lawsuits.”
Bis also pointed to President Donald Trump’s remarks to CBS News about Good from January, in which he said “I love all of our people … and I would bet you that she, under normal circumstances, was a very solid, wonderful person. But, you know, her actions were pretty tough.” Trump also defended ICE, saying the job of federal agents was “being made very difficult.”
CNN has reached out to DHS, and phone numbers listed under Noem’s name for comment. Bovino declined to comment about the lawsuit.
The lawsuit alleges the shots fired by Ross were “the predictable and intended product of the operation,” according to the family’s attorneys.
The lawsuit seeks unspecified compensatory and punitive damages.
Good’s partner and plaintiff, Becca Good, spoke publicly for the first time since the deadly shooting took place. During the Thursday news conference, she called Good “the center” of her universe and spoke about taking their 6-year-old son to first grade without her.
“Living without her is like trying to live without the sun. And you don’t know how much light something gives you until it’s gone, and then you feel that absence every single second,” she said, becoming emotional.
Renee Good loved her three children, her partner said, and enjoyed reading them books, and talking about music and comics with them.
“Every morning, she is my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” she said. “But I also think a lot about what she would have wanted after all of this.”
Becca Good said the family is pursuing legal action because “Renee’s love and legacy demand a better world for her children, for this community, and for this country.”
“What happened to us should never happen to any family,” Good said. “Accountability and change — true accountability — is the only way to make sure that no other family has to go through what we have.”
“I don’t hate the people who took Renee from us, but what I want them to understand is - every single day, they get to look at their children, and their wives, and their sisters, and know what they took from our family,” Good said. “They took a mother away from her children. They know that, and they will carry it forever.”
Good, a mother of three , had just finished dropping her 6-year-old son off at school when she encountered ICE agents.
The moments leading up to the shooting were captured by bystanders as well as Ross , a 10-year ICE veteran, whose cellphone video starts with him in front of Good’s burgundy SUV . The vehicle was stopped for a few minutes perpendicular to a snowy residential Minneapolis street, obstructing the flow of traffic.
Ross did not say anything as he walked from the front of the car toward the driver’s side.
Good then addressed Ross, the video shows.
“That’s fine, dude. I’m not mad at you,” she says. Ross didn’t respond.
Becca Good was standing outside the car and said “show your face” to Ross, whose masked reflection is seen on the vehicle’s windows as he continues walking around it. Becca Good holds her cellphone up, seemingly recording Ross, and tells him, “You wanna come at us? You wanna come at us? I say go get yourself some lunch, big boy.”
She then tries to get back into the car, but the door is locked.
Another officer then tells Renee Good to “get out of the f**king car.”
Renee Good is then seen reversing the car and glancing forward as she turns the steering wheel to the right. The car moves forward, Ross cries out, “whoa,” and three gunshots are heard. Good was shot shortly after 9:30 a.m., according to a news release from the city government.
The video filmed by Ross captured audio of gunshots but doesn’t show the actual moment of the shooting, though other video from bystanders shows Ross was standing out of the vehicle’s path when he opened fire. He fired first into her windshield and then at close range through the open driver’s side window, videos show .
The end of Ross’s video shows the SUV as it barrels forward. Someone can be heard saying, “f**king b*tch.”
DHS later said Good “weaponized her vehicle” to run over an officer near an ICE vehicle.
The search for accountability for the shooting remains ongoing. In March , the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office and two state agencies sued the Trump administration for access to evidence in Good’s shooting death as well as the death of Alex Pretti, who was killed by DHS agents in January.
In July, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced the Department of Justice had provided a trove of materials related to both shootings to state investigators. No charges have been filed in either case.

The National Capital Planning Commission on Thursday unanimously voted to approve building plans for a new White House Visitor Screening Facility.
The project is part of President Donald Trump’s massive overhaul of the White House grounds, but one that has enjoyed bipartisan support and drawn little pushback compared to his other construction plans.
The facility will be built off 15th Street in Sherman Park, with an entrance that leads below ground for screening and allows visitors to exit by the East Wing of the White House, the site of the president’s more controversial ballroom project.
The commission’s chairman, Trump appointee Mark Paoletta, said Thursday, “I look forward to the beautiful building be built on the White House grounds.”
Lee Webb, an urban planner with the 12-member commission, presented the final plans for the facility. He said it will include a versatile indoor open-floor-plan space that will allow the Secret Service to install permanent screening technology. The space will also allow significant indoor queuing for large events, with a 700-person occupancy within the screening facility.
Visitors to the White House are now screened in temporary, double-wide trailers and tents, which the Secret Service has said falls short of its security needs.
The plans were approved by all members of the commission, which includes representatives appointed by Washington Mayor Muriel Bowser, a Democrat.
Construction work is expected to begin in the next month and finish at some point in 2028.
Representing the General Services Administration on the board, Trump appointee Paul Ingrassia hailed the addition of the new facility as “an incredible part of this White House reimagining we’ve been seeing.”
That includes the massive 90,000-square-foot ballroom that’s being constructed at the site of the former East Wing. The commission approved the plans for the ballroom in April.
At Thursday’s hearing, one of the presenters said the exit of the new facility will have Corinthian columns to “align with the ballroom’s language.”
The president has been highly involved in renovations at the White House, which have included gold adornments in the Oval Office and the installation of a helipad on the White House lawn, as well as other projects around D.C., like the proposed construction of a “ Triumphal Arch .”

articles.title_orig: Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
articles.title_zh: Cornell Jane Doe's attorney says she told police in 2024: 'I was raped'
articles.content_orig:
Students walk on the campus of Cornell University on Wednesday in Ithaca, N.Y. Spencer Platt/Getty Images hide caption
The woman who alleges she was gang raped by fellow Cornell University students in 2024 clearly stated in her statement to police two years ago that she was sexually assaulted.
That's according to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, who confirmed to NPR that his client told investigators, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," citing transcripts from Jane Doe's sworn statement in 2024.
NPR asked Giuffra to specifically confirm on the record to NPR that his client made this exact quoted statement regarding her assault. His response by text: "Yes she did."
This is in contrast to statements from the local prosecutor, who claimed on Monday that Doe never stated she was raped. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten told NPR local station WSKG on Wednesday that he had not read the full account of her detailed statements to investigators where she repeatedly described being assaulted.
NPR asked Cornell if campus police provided the DA with all of the information from their investigation, including her repeated statements about being assaulted. The university did not respond to the request for comment.
CBS News New York reported Wednesday on a transcript of an interview between the Cornell University Police Department investigator and the alleged victim. NPR has not been able to obtain a copy of these transcripts.
Van Houten said in Monday's statement that in the 2024 statement taken by Cornell University police, Doe "did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual."
No criminal charges were ever filed against the seven men Doe alleges drugged and assaulted her for several hours in October 2024.
Van Houten told NPR member station WSKG on Wednesday evening that he was in the process of getting the interview transcript from Cornell. He told the station over email that he doesn't know when he will get the transcript from the university "or if Cornell will resist turning it over."
"If it's factual, we absolutely should have been informed about what Jane Doe said to police that was not in her six-page statement," he told WSKG.
Van Houten said earlier this week that his office is reexamining the case.
He added that particular transcript is part of the confidential Title IX investigation Cornell launched into the alleged assault.
In mid-September, Doe filed a lawsuit against the seven men who she alleges assaulted her two years ago. Cornell was also named in the lawsuit.
Following the onslaught of public backlash against Cornell and the local prosecutor, the school said Wednesday night that it will bring in an outside counsel to conduct an independent probe into the handling of the case.
Since Tuesday, Cornell has directed the public to an FAQ page on the rape allegations.
The university has maintained that Cornell University Police investigated the case thoroughly and that the school held its own Title IX investigation, which resulted in suspensions and expulsions. Cornell has not specified how many students faced punishments, or of what nature. It noted in the FAQ: "Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response."
WSKG found that as of Wednesday, the university has changed its FAQ. And it has quietly removed a sentence stating that the Cornell police "shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office."
Previously, the FAQ read: "The Cornell University Police Department investigated the matter in 2024 and shared all investigatory information with the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office, which is the established protocol if the department believes it is possible a crime has occurred."
But by Wednesday afternoon , WSKG found that statement had been edited, and any mention of Cornell police sharing "all investigatory information" with the district attorney had disappeared from the page.
"The Cornell University Police Department is a unit of the university, and its officers are sworn Tompkins County deputy sheriffs whose duties include the enforcement of law and order on Cornell property," the new statement reads. "This incident occurred in Cornell's jurisdiction."
WSKG reported that Cornell University did not respond to its questions about these changes.
Students at the university have expressed outrage and deep disappointment toward school officials for their handling of this case. The Cornell University Student Assembly scheduled a public hearing set for Thursday afternoon during which they say they will "demand institutional accountability" from their school.
"We stand unequivocally with survivors of sexual violence, and we remain committed to ensuring that their voices are not only heard, but met with action," the organization said in a statement on Instagram .
Late Wednesday, the school confirmed to NPR that it is bringing in an outside counsel to hold an independent examination of the alleged gang rape.
University officials told NPR they have no further details about how the investigation will play out. Previously, Cornell strongly defended how it handled the case when Doe first reported the incident to school officials two years ago.
The move comes after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul called for the school to open an outside investigation. In a video posted on X , Hochul also said she's considering new legislation to tighten sexual assault laws across the state.
"While we have some of the toughest laws on sexual assault on college campuses right here in New York, I think we can do better," she said. "This culture has to stop. And it will stop here in the state of New York."
WSKG's Aurora Berry contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.title_zh: What happened in the failed execution of Christa Pike - and what next?
articles.content_orig:
What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
US convicted murderer Christa Pike is in a critical condition in hospital after Tennessee authorities failed to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyer says.
The case of Pike, whose attempted execution on Wednesday had already been the subject of a high-profile legal battle, has raised a number of questions.
These include what went wrong, what happens next, and - for opponents of the death penalty - fresh concerns around the suffering of an inmate when an execution does not go to plan.
A review into what happened has been ordered and executions in Tennessee have been halted for the rest of the year, Governor Bill Lee said.
Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, an attack that was carried out alongside her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp, who was 17. Shipp remains in prison, having been spared the death penalty under state law.
Pike was scheduled to be put to death in Tennessee on Wednesday evening local time. The injections were allowed by the Supreme Court at the eleventh hour after the legal battle.
Pike was given two injections of the drug pentobarbital but her legal team said these failed to stop her heartbeat and that she could still be heard snoring.
Watch: Witnesses recount Christa Pike's failed execution attempt
Tennessee halts executions after death row inmate Christa Pike survives hers
US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections
The Tennessee Department of Correction has defended the method it used, saying "the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out."
The state protocol does not clearly specify what should happen if an inmate remains alive after a second dose, according to the AP news agency.
Authorities are yet to say whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have yet to give their explanation of why the dosage given to Pike was non-fatal, although medical experts have given theories.
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, told the BBC Pike probably never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause her breath to stop or heart failure.
The Tennessee correction department said Pike had been taken to an off-site medical facility, while one of her lawyers said on Wednesday that she was being given "life-saving measures" in hospital.
On Thursday, lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters: "We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment."
He added: "But we do know that that she is alive right now."
In his emailed comments to the BBC, Zivot said: "It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury."
A third-party review has been ordered by state Governor Bill Lee, who said on Thursday that Tennessee will halt executions for the rest of the year.
This could impact any additional attempt by the state to execute Pike in the near-term, if she does regain consciousness.
May Martinez, the mother of Colleen Slemmer who had pushed for Pike's execution to take place, told NBC News the events had been "a mess".
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed by Pike and her boyfriend
Historically, the US Supreme Court has not halted second attempts at executions, said John Mills, a lawyer who works with inmates sentenced to death.
In 2024, it allowed Alabama to proceed with a second execution of Kenneth Eugene Smith, using an experimental oxygen deprivation method, after their attempt to kill him by lethal injection failed two years before.
A notable Supreme Court case from 1947 allowed the state of Louisiana to try a second electrocution of Willie Smith, a black teenager whose first execution attempt failed when he was 17 years old.
The court found a second execution would not violate the Constitution's prohibitions against double jeopardy or cruel and unusual punishment and Smith was executed aged 18.
"If the question is, is it likely the federal courts would intervene in a second attempt? I'm afraid the answer is a resounding no," Mills said of Pike's case.
Pike's lawyers have already filed a motion to stay her execution.
Mills said that if he was her lawyer, he would be asking both the federal courts and Tennessee court to reconsider their views on a second attempt and would also approach Governor Lee, who has powers to issue stays of executions and exercise clemency.
Opponents of the death penalty have been quick to react.
Maya Foa, the head of international legal organisation Reprieve, said: "We cannot know exactly what went wrong, because so much happened behind a curtain â lethal injection relies on secrecy at every stage, to hide the violence of the state taking a human life."
Pentobarbital is a potent sedative that slows down the body, including the nervous system. Doctors sometimes use it as a treatment for certain conditions but in high doses it can also be used as a lethal injection to cause death.
Its use in lethal injections came under renewed scrutiny last year after a US federal government review during the Biden administration raised concerns about the drug's potential for "unnecessary pain and suffering".
The Biden government banned its use in federal executions but that did not bind individual states such as Tennessee, which can choose their own methods.
Why the death penalty is on the rise in US
In recent years, states have found some drugs needed for lethal injections harder to come by, because pharmaceutical companies have opposed the use of their products for such purposes.
Some manufacturers have explicitly said they will no longer produce pentobarbital or will restrict their use in executions, according to Alexis Hoag-Fordjor, Co-Director of the Center for Criminal Justice at Brooklyn Law School.
In 2024, for instance, the manufacturer Absolute Standards said it would no longer make the drug. , external
The Tennessee correction department has not specifically addressed an allegation from Pike's legal team that the pentobarbital it used was "degraded". Drugs may degrade for a number of reasons, including if it has aged beyond its use-by date and its potency has decreased.
But the department issued a broader defence of its method, writing in a statement: "The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective."
"It's unclear, the quality and the effectiveness of the drug" used in Pike's execution, Hoag-Fordjor told the BBC, given how difficult it has been for states like Tennessee to obtain pentobarbital.
"It shouldn't be a surprise something went wrong," he said.
The predicament Tennessee authorities found themselves in - having to call emergency medical services to save Pike after trying to kill her - suggested there was "no plan in place" for a scenario like Pike's, Hoag-Fordjor added.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in Tennessee in 2026 that did not go to plan.
The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal injection. He was given a one-year reprieve by Governor Bill Lee.
More widely across the US, the issue of botched executions continues to cause alarm.
In 2022, more than a third of executions in the US were botched or highly problematic, according to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPI) - an organisation that provides statistics and research on the death penalty but does not take a stance on it morally.

In 204, the execution of Clayton Lockett was postponed after 20 minutes because a lethal injection of three drugs failed to work properly when one of his veins ruptured and he went on to writhe and shake uncontrollably.
